name: Djiboutian Skoudehkaris
description: Skoudehkaris, Djibouti's real national dish, is genuinely built on a full, warm spice blend - cumin, cardamom, cinnamon, and cloves together with lamb and rice - real technique braising the meat first until tender before the rice cooks directly in that same spiced broth, absorbing everything.
steps_detailed: Brown the lamb with the onion and garlic, 8-9 minutes.
Add the tomato paste and cook 2 minutes, then add the tomatoes, cumin, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, and bay leaf.
Add 1.25 cups water and simmer 25-28 minutes until the meat is tender.
Stir in the rice, cover, and simmer 18-20 minutes until tender, absorbing the spiced broth.

name: Djiboutian Fah-fah
description: Fah-fah, a hearty spiced meat soup, is a beloved Djiboutian comfort dish, especially popular in the south near the Somali border - real versions genuinely include leeks and cabbage alongside potato, not just a plain meat broth, with green chili for real heat. Real goat is used directly here, since it's genuinely available at halal, Caribbean, and Latin American markets across the US.
steps_detailed: Simmer the goat in 2.5 cups water 30-35 minutes until nearly tender.
Add the leeks, cabbage, potato, jalapeño, and tomatoes, and simmer 18-20 minutes more until everything is tender.
steps: Simmer the goat in 2.5 cups water 30-35 minutes until nearly tender.

name: Djiboutian Lahoh
description: Lahoh (also called canjeero), a spongy, fermented flatbread with a real honeycomb-bubbled surface, is a Djiboutian breakfast staple, real technique letting the batter ferment before cooking undisturbed on one side only.
steps_detailed: Whisk the flour, cornmeal, and baking powder with enough water to form a thin, smooth batter.
Let ferment at room temperature 3-4 hours until slightly bubbly.
Pour a thin layer into a hot, lightly oiled non-stick pan, and cook, uncovered, without flipping, 2-3 minutes, until bubbles form across the entire surface and the top is set.

name: Djiboutian Sabayaad
description: Sabayaad, a layered flatbread, reflects Djibouti's real Yemeni and Somali culinary influence, real technique coiling the dough before flattening to build real flaky layers.
steps_detailed: Work the flour with warm water and half the oil into a soft dough. Rest 20 minutes.
Roll thin, brush with the remaining oil, and coil before flattening again to build real layers.
Cook in a hot, dry pan, 2-3 minutes per side, until golden.

name: Djiboutian Fish with Rice
description: A fragrant fish and rice dish, real technique poaching the fish directly in the tomato-spiced rice broth so it absorbs the flavor as it cooks.
steps_detailed: Cook the garlic and cumin in a little oil 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes and 1.25 cups water, and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Stir in the rice, cover, and simmer 15 minutes, then nestle the fish on top and cook 8-10 minutes more, covered, until the fish is just cooked through and the rice is tender.

name: Djiboutian Sambusas
description: Sambusas, fried triangular pastries with a spiced filling, reflect real Yemeni and Indian culinary influence, a beloved Djiboutian snack.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef with the onion and cumin, 6-7 minutes.
Cut the phyllo into strips, fill, and fold into triangles.
Fry, turning, 3-4 minutes, until deeply golden.

name: Djiboutian Yetakelt Wat
description: Yetakelt wat, a spicy mixed vegetable stew shared with Ethiopian tradition, real technique building real depth from a proper berbere base.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion and berbere in a little oil, 3-4 minutes.
Add the potato, carrot, and green beans with a splash of water, and simmer 20-22 minutes until tender.

name: Djiboutian Spiced Tea (Shah Hawaash)
description: Spiced tea with cardamom and cinnamon is central to Djiboutian daily hospitality, real technique steeping the whole spices directly with the tea.
steps_detailed: Warm the tea with the milk, cardamom, and cinnamon 5-6 minutes.
Stir in the sugar before serving.

name: Djiboutian Grilled Fish
description: Grilled fish rubbed with garlic and lemon, reflecting Djibouti's real Red Sea and Gulf of Aden coastal tradition.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and lemon juice, and let sit 10 minutes.
Grill or broil, 4-5 minutes per side, until just cooked through.
